title: Precision, held in a mold.
subtitle: One carefully made form. A shape that can be repeated.
summary: Watch a multipart mold separate from a stepped H-block. The proposed trick is to make the difficult geometry in the form, while the stone is still workable.
sceneDescription: A gray H-shaped stone with stepped recesses, surrounded by an exploded timber mold and removable inserts.
modelNote: An invented mold around a simplified H-block. This is a geometric study, not a measured reconstruction of a particular artifact.

steps.name: Assemble
steps.title: Put the precision in the form.
steps.text: Timber sides and removable inserts define the outside edges and recessed faces. Making an accurate, reusable form is the first engineering challenge.

steps.name: Pack
steps.title: Work the material into every corner.
steps.text: A hypothetical mineral mixture fills the spaces around the inserts. The animation prescribes the fill; it does not calculate flow or trapped air.

steps.name: Set
steps.title: Let the shape become self-supporting.
steps.text: The material must develop enough strength to survive release. Shrinkage, surface finish, and recipe are questions for a physical trial.

steps.name: Release
steps.title: Take the mold apart, piece by piece.
steps.text: Side panels move outward and the recessed inserts withdraw from the face. A workable mold needs a release path for every piece.

steps.name: Inspect
steps.title: Read the finished surface.
steps.text: The mold transfers its geometry to the block. Look for repeatable imperfections, seams, and surface texture that could distinguish a cast surface from a worked one.

issues.title: Sharp internal corners
issues.mechanism: An insert can form a recess while the material is soft, reducing the amount of hard-stone removal needed afterward.
issues.remaining: The insert itself still needs accurate manufacture and a practical release direction.

issues.title: Repeated geometry
issues.mechanism: Reusing a mold could reproduce both the intended shape and small accidental details.
issues.remaining: Similar shapes alone do not show mold reuse. Surveyed dimensions and repeated defects would be more informative.

hypothesis: Davidovits and colleagues propose an artificial origin for sampled Pumapunku andesite. This study explores one possible molding arrangement; their materials claim does not establish this particular mold.
alternative: Skilled stoneworking with templates, pecking, grinding, and abrasion can also produce regular geometry. The relevant comparison is the actual surface and internal structure of the stone.
test: Make several blocks from the same multipart mold. Measure dimensional variation, release damage, seams, and repeated surface defects; compare them with documented H-blocks.
